mainEntity.name: What is a good margin for a wholesaler?

acceptedAnswer.text: Judge the blend, not the best line. Food distribution runs thin, and a book holding 19.5% across staples and specialty is doing better than one quoting 25.9% on a third of its sales.

mainEntity.name: What is the average markup from wholesale to retail?

acceptedAnswer.text: It varies by category and by what the retailer needs to clear. Work it from their end: take the margin they require on the shelf and check the wholesale price that leaves them.
Each tier's margin weighted by its share of sales. Staples at 15.3% across 60% of sales and specialty at 25.9% across the rest come to 19.5%.

mainEntity.name: Why is a 35% markup only a 25.9% margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: The $7.70 of profit is the same either way. Markup divides it by the $22.00 you paid; margin divides it by the $29.70 you charged, and the bigger denominator gives the smaller number.

mainEntity.name: Should staples carry the same markup as specialty?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rarely. They are price-checked constantly, so they carry less. What matters is knowing the share of sales running through them, because that is what sets the blend.

mainEntity.name: How do you lift a blended margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Move sales mix before you move price. A point of sales shifting from staples to specialty does more for the blend than a point on the staple markup.

mainEntity.name: Should a markup go on the supplier price or the landed cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Landed cost, always. Freight and handling are in the case before you price it, so marking up the invoice leaves that money uncollected on every case you sell.
